images.filename: The "Survivor Tree", Campsie Playing Fields, Omagh - geograph.org.uk - 602209.jpg
images.caption: The "Survivor Tree", Campsie Playing Fields, Omagh I once called this very ancient tree the survivor tree because it withstood various alterations to the surrounding terrain and drastic tree surgery, but looking at the hollow in the centre, more apparent now with the leaves almost all off, it makes you wonder how much longer it can survive. It must have witnessed some historical events in its time, including the alleged passage of King James over the site of King James Bridge on his way to the Siege of Derry.

images.caption: Orange arch, Omagh. How shall I delicately put this - Not "Londonderry"? In actual fact the names refer to the siege of Derry, Battle of Aughrim, Enniskillen and Battle of the Boyne. Derry, the original name of Londonderry, and is derived from Doire, the "place of oaks." More at Derry.

images.filename: The Verbal Arts Centre from the Double Bastion - geograph.org.uk - 1515912.jpg
images.caption: The Verbal Arts Centre from the Double Bastion This image has been taken from near Roaring Meg, seen on the left, at 1794kg, the largest of the Londonderry canons. It was deployed during the siege of 1689. The Verbal Arts building wasn't previously the First Derry National School.

images.filename: Derry St Columb's Cathedral Choirboys' Vestry Siege Window Upper Lights 2013 09 17.jpg
images.caption: Upper lights of the stained glass window in the south wall of the choirboys' vestry, depicting the Siege of Derry in 1689. Unfortunately, the lower lights were hidden behind a wardrobe when this photograph was taken. The window was created by Powell & Sons and unveiled on 31 July 1913. (See  Irish Times 1 August 1913, p. 6, and J. Godfrey F. Day and Henry E. Patton: The Cathedrals of the Church of Ireland, p. 36–37.)
